opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons, and they mostly come down to how you actually want to work alongside an agent.

The first is just practical: if the agent is sharing your screen, you can't use your computer while it's working. It's moving the mouse, typing, clicking around, and you're sitting there with your hands off the keyboard watching it. That kills most of the value. The whole point of delegating a task is that you get to go do something else. If it has its own machine, a VM or a container with its own display, you can hand it a task, go back to your own work, and check in on it like you would with a coworker.

The second is safety and blast radius. On your own computer the agent has access to everything you're logged into: your email, your bank, your files. Even if the model is well-behaved, it can misclick, misread something, or get confused by a prompt injection on some random webpage. In a sandboxed environment you control exactly what it can touch. You give it the credentials and tools it needs for that task and nothing more, and if something goes wrong you throw the environment away and start over.

Third, it's just a cleaner environment for the model. Your desktop has notifications popping up, a dozen windows open, all your personal setup. A fresh, consistent screen is much easier for the model to reason about, and it makes runs more reproducible, which matters a lot when you're debugging why an agent failed or trying to evaluate it.

And finally, it scales. Once the agent has its own computer, there's no reason it has to be one. You can spin up five or ten of them running in parallel on different tasks, which you could never do if they all had to share your one screen. That starts to feel less like a tool you're operating and more like a small team you're managing.

r001.rationale: Says that with its own machine, the user can hand the agent a task and go back to their own work while it runs.

r002.rationale: Describes checking in on the agent’s separate machine while it works, equivalent to periodically checking a remote machine.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the simplest way to put it is that a computer-use agent is not a thing that sits quietly in a text box. It's actually moving the mouse and typing on the keyboard. So if it's on the same machine you're using, the moment it starts working, you basically have to take your hands off. You can't check Slack, you can't open another window, because every click you make is either going to be interpreted by the agent as something weird happening on screen, or you're going to interrupt it mid-action. It turns into this really awkward handoff where you're just watching it the whole time.

And that undermines the whole point. The reason you want an agent doing this stuff is so you can go do something else. If it has its own machine, or its own virtual desktop, you can kick off a task, go back to your own work, and come back later. It becomes much more like delegating to a coworker than like sharing a steering wheel.

The second reason is just safety and containment. These models still make mistakes. They'll click the wrong button, they'll open the wrong tab, occasionally they'll do something you really didn't want. If it's on your actual computer with your logged-in accounts, your files, your email, the blast radius of a mistake is your entire digital life. If it's on a sandboxed environment, you can scope exactly what it has access to. You give it the browser and the one app it needs, and if it goes sideways, you just throw the environment away.

And honestly, from a development point of view, a separate screen is also just much cleaner to observe. You can record it, you can replay what it did, you can see every screenshot it took and every action it chose. That's really useful for debugging, and it's much harder to do that when the agent's actions are tangled up with whatever you were doing at the same time.

So it's really three things: you keep your own machine usable, you limit what can go wrong, and you get a much clearer view of what the agent is actually doing.

r001.rationale: It says a separate machine or virtual desktop lets the user start a task and return to their own work while the agent works.

r002.rationale: It says the user can come back later, but does not frame the interaction as periodically checking in on a remote machine.

astra-6.text: The big reason is that you want it to work in parallel with you. If the agent is using your mouse and keyboard, you’re sort of sitting there watching it, because the moment you try to do something else, you interfere with what it’s doing. Giving it its own screen means you can hand off a task and keep working. It also creates a clearer boundary: you can give it the apps and accounts it needs without giving it access to everything on your personal computer.

r001.rationale: It says the user can hand off a task to the agent and keep working while it uses its own screen.

r002.rationale: It describes working in parallel, but does not frame interaction as periodically checking in on a remote machine.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that you want it to work in parallel with you. If an agent is using your mouse and keyboard, you’re basically sitting there watching it, because the moment you try to do something else, you’re fighting over the cursor. Giving it its own screen means you can hand off a task and keep working.

It also gives you a nice isolation boundary. You can choose which accounts it’s logged into and what information it can access, instead of exposing everything on your personal computer. And if it gets stuck, you can look at its screen, help it out, and then let it keep going.

r001.rationale: It says a separate screen lets the user hand off a task and keep working while the agent works.

r002.rationale: It mentions looking at the agent’s screen if it gets stuck, but does not frame interaction as periodically checking in on a remote machine.
